e.etymology: A short form of Alexander, and of Alexis and Alexandra, from Greek alexein, 'to defend', and aner, 'man'. It is an everyday name in the Netherlands.

assoc.t: Lex Luthor, Superman's archenemy
lex, the Latin word for law

e.etymology: A z spelling of Isabel, the medieval Spanish and Occitan form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, 'my God is an oath'. The spelling is found in Brazil and in the US.
A modern American name, either Marie with an A- prefix or a feminine spelling of Amari. It peaked in 2005, when the R&B singer Amerie was on the charts.
From an English surname taken from places called Rockwell, usually explained as Old English hroc, 'rook', plus wella, 'spring, stream'. Most Americans know it through the painter Norman Rockwell.

assoc.t: Norman Rockwell, painter of small-town America
Rockwell Automation, industrial equipment maker
Rockwell, singer of Somebody's Watching Me

e.etymology: From the English word for soft, napped leather, shortened from French gants de Suede, 'gloves of Sweden'. A recent American word name, used mostly for boys.

assoc.t: suede, the soft napped leather
Blue Suede Shoes, Elvis Presley rock and roll classic

e.etymology: From azan, the Urdu and Persian form of Arabic adhan, the Muslim call to prayer. As a given name it is used mostly by South Asian Muslim families.
A modern spelling of Michaela shaped by Mc- surnames such as McKenzie. Michaela is the feminine form of Michael, Hebrew for 'who is like God?'.
namesakes: McKayla Maroney (Olympic gymnast of the 'not impressed' meme)

e.etymology: An American spelling of Marquis, the French title of nobility, originally the lord of a march or border territory. As a first name it is mostly African American and peaked in the 1990s.
namesakes: Marquise Brown (NFL wide receiver nicknamed Hollywood)

assoc.t: marquise, a pointed-oval diamond cut
marquise, French title for the wife of a marquis

e.note: In French, marquise is the feminine title; the male form is marquis.

e.etymology: A spelling of Coby or Kobi, short forms of Jacob, and of Kobe. American use peaked in 2000 as Kobe Bryant rose to stardom with the Lakers.

assoc.t: Kobe Bryant, Lakers legend (spelled Kobe)

e.meaning: form of Helen; perhaps torch or shining light
e.etymology: The Romanian form of Helen, from Greek Helene, a name of uncertain meaning often linked to words for torch or light. Ileana Cosanzeana is the fairy-tale princess of Romanian folklore.
A phonetic spelling of Ciara as Americans say it, see-AR-uh, and sometimes of Sierra. Ciara is an Irish name from ciar, 'dark, black', said KEER-uh in Ireland.

assoc.t: Ciara, R&B singer (spelled with a C)

e.etymology: From the German surname Kolbe, a variant of Kolb, from a word for a club or mace. Catholic families use it for Saint Maximilian Kolbe, the Polish priest who died at Auschwitz; it also serves as a spelling of Colby.

assoc.t: Saint Maximilian Kolbe, priest martyred at Auschwitz

e.etymology: A respelling of Delilah, from Hebrew Delilah, usually read as 'delicate' or 'languishing'. In the Book of Judges, Delilah learns the secret of Samson's strength and betrays him.

assoc.t: Delilah, who betrays Samson in the Bible
Hey There Delilah, 2006 hit by the Plain White T's

e.etymology: From Hebrew Mordokhay, of unknown origin; a leading theory ties it to Marduk, the chief god of Babylon. In the Book of Esther, Mordecai is Esther's cousin and guardian, a hero of the Purim story.
namesakes: Mordecai (the blue jay of Cartoon Network's Regular Show)

assoc.t: Mordecai, Esther's guardian in the Bible's Purim story
Mordecai, blue jay of the cartoon Regular Show

e.etymology: From Arabic rahma, 'mercy, compassion', from the same root as two of the best-known names of God in Islam, al-Rahman and al-Rahim.
Usually listed as a Swahili name; it is close to Hasani, the Swahili form of Arabic Hasan. Its use for American boys and girls is recent.
A simplified spelling of Soleil, the French word for sun, from Latin sol. Soleil has been an American girls' name since the 1980s.

assoc.t: Cirque du Soleil, the circus company (same word)

e.etymology: From Arabic anisa, 'friendly, good company', the feminine of Anis. In Southeast Asia the similar Annisa is taken from an-nisa, 'the women', the title of a chapter of the Quran.
From Arabic raniya, 'gazing, looking at'. It is best known through Queen Rania of Jordan. In Greece, Rania is a short form of Ourania.
namesakes: Queen Rania of Jordan (wife of King Abdullah II)

assoc.t: Queen Rania of Jordan

e.etymology: A name with several sources: a Finnish variant of Mikko, a form of Michael; a Slavic pet form of names such as Mikolaj (Nicholas); and a Japanese girls' name written with various kanji. In the US it is given mostly to boys.

assoc.t: miko, a shrine maiden in Japanese Shinto
Meeko, the raccoon in Disney's Pocahontas

e.etymology: A spelling of Kaylee favored in Spanish-speaking families, where ey writes the English long a. Kaylee is a modern American blend of Kay and Lee.

e.meaning: city; the holy city of Medina
e.etymology: From Arabic al-madina, 'the city', the name of Medina, the city of the Prophet Muhammad. As a girls' name it is most common in Central Asia and the Caucasus.

assoc.t: Medina, Islam's second holiest city, in Saudi Arabia

e.etymology: From the English word, which came through Old French pais from Latin pax. It was among the Puritan virtue names and today is especially common in West African Christian families.

assoc.t: peace, a casual way to say goodbye

e.etymology: A respelling of Kingston, an English place name and surname from Old English cyning, 'king', and tun, 'town, estate'. The y is a modern American touch.

assoc.t: Kingston, capital of Jamaica (spelled Kingston)
Kingston memory cards and flash drives

e.etymology: A streamlined American spelling of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques, which goes back through James to Hebrew Yaakov, Jacob, 'holder of the heel'.
The feminine of Manuel, the Spanish and Portuguese short form of Emmanuel, from Hebrew Immanuel, 'God is with us'.
From the Welsh surname meaning 'son of Evan'. Evan is the English form of Welsh Ifan, a form of John. As a first name Evans is also common in Kenya and Ghana.
A spelling of Liliana that shows the nickname Lilly. Liliana is a Latinate elaboration of Lily and Lilian, from Latin lilium, the lily flower.
From the capital of Norway. The city's Old Norse name is usually read as 'meadow below the ridge' or 'meadow of the gods'. American parents took it up in the 2010s, in step with Otto and Arlo.

assoc.t: Oslo, capital of Norway
Oslo Accords, 1990s Israeli-Palestinian peace deals

e.meaning: free man; also a joyful song
e.etymology: A short form of Caroline, the feminine of Carolus, Latin for Charles, from Germanic karl, 'free man'. English speakers also hear the word carol, a song of joy. It was a top-ten American girls' name in the 1940s.
namesakes: Carol Brady (the mother on The Brady Bunch)

assoc.t: carol, a Christmas song
A Christmas Carol, Dickens's holiday story

e.etymology: A respelling of Aidan, the English form of Irish Aodhan, a pet form of Aodh, 'fire'. Saint Aidan of Lindisfarne brought Christianity to northern England in the 7th century.
The German and Scandinavian spelling of Theodore, from Greek Theodoros: theos, 'god', plus doron, 'gift'.
